version.changelog: The helper now waits for your approval, and if you approve after it has stopped waiting, Beatra connects automatically the next time you use it, with no second approval.

llm.summary: The skill is a real shift-handoff voice workflow, but it asks for broader Beatra account authority and silent package updates than the narrow voice-clip purpose needs.

dimensions.detail: The skill makes network calls to Beatra, uploads local clone samples only when requested, writes local state under ~/.beatra, and can query wallet/task data; these are partly purpose-aligned but broader than needed for voice clips.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Installation and authorization are disclosed, but they create a shared full-scope Device Token in ~/.beatra/credentials.json and run a non-billable registration call; this is high-impact account access for a narrow skill.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions require using a bundled generic MCP client that can list and call arbitrary Beatra tools by name, not only fixed voice-related operations.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The bundled client silently checks daily and can automatically replace package-owned files from Beatra update endpoints. The updater has integrity/path checks and can be disabled, but silent self-update materially expands post-review behavior.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The stated purpose is generating 8 to 20 shift-handoff voice clips, and the workflow mostly matches that, but the authorization scope also covers image, video, music, artifact, wallet, task-cancel, and broad MCP tool access beyond voice generation.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable granting this package a broad Beatra device authorization, storing a shared bearer token under ~/.beatra, and allowing the bundled client to contact Beatra and silently update package-owned files unless you disable auto-updates. This is not evidence of malware, but it deserves review because the granted capabilities exceed the advertised voice-clip task.
llm.findings:
[SDI-2] unexpected: Accepted in context: artifact code requests generation scopes for images, videos, and music even though the skill workflow only needs speech, voice, upload/model/task, and billing-related access.
[SDI-1] unexpected: Accepted in context: the bundled MCP client exposes generic tools/list and tools/call plus account and task operations, which is broader than a fixed shift-handoff voice workflow.
[PE3] expected: Partly downgraded: reading ~/.beatra/credentials.json is expected for the declared device-bearer connection and includes permission checks, but the credential is full-scope and shared across Beatra skills, so users should treat it as sensitive account access.
[RA1] unexpected: Accepted in context: self-update is disclosed and constrained to fixed Beatra URLs with manifest and checksum verification, but automatic code replacement is not required for creating voice clips.
[TP4] expected: Partly downgraded: uninstall, disconnect, token revocation, and shared-state inventory are disclosed lifecycle flows for shared Beatra auth rather than hidden runtime behavior, but they increase the skill's administrative reach.
[LP3] unexpected: Accepted in context: there is no narrow tool allowlist; the package relies on a generic local client and a broad remote authorization.
[AIG SARIF] expected: The supplied A.I.G SARIF run reported no results, so it did not independently validate malicious behavior.
